Senses.Explanation: An adverb meaning 'on the spot' or 'immediately.' Chan texts place it before getting it, becoming a buddha, awakening, and verdicts such as 'a dead fellow on the spot.' A master says, 'I now wait for you to get it on the spot,' without added effort. The recurring Chan bend is the demand for the event or verdict right where the person is, rather than at another place or a deferred time.
Senses.Note: Primary adverbial sense. Exact posture uses are separated below; the previously included 'the buddhas stand listening' witness belongs there, not here.

Occurrences.Kwic: 我如今立地待汝搆去。更不教汝加功煉行
Occurrences.AttributionNote: The master says he now waits for the addressee to get it on the spot and will not require further effort.

Occurrences.Kwic: 不見汾陽人，盡是立地死漢
Occurrences.AttributionNote: Those who do not see the person of Fenyang are called dead fellows on the spot.

Occurrences.Kwic: 屠子立地成佛，不名性燥
Occurrences.AttributionNote: A hall address uses the stock figure of the butcher becoming a buddha on the spot.

Occurrences.Kwic: 你諸人而今忽若立地悟去，莫道生死以至十方虗空悉皆消殞
Occurrences.AttributionNote: An address says that if the listeners were to awaken on the spot, birth and death and the ten directions would all disappear.

Senses.Explanation: The literal posture of standing at a place. A hall address tells the assembly not to stand there dozing; the flame sermon has the buddhas of the three times stand and listen; another speaker says, 'I now stand here watching you.' These describe bodily posture and location, not immediate occurrence.
Senses.Note: Physical-posture referent, independently anchored across three texts. Larger compounds such as 'stand upright between heaven and earth' remain outside this narrower entry.

Occurrences.Kwic: 你諸人休向者裏立地瞌睡
Occurrences.AttributionNote: The assembly is told not to stand here dozing, an unambiguously postural use.

Occurrences.Kwic: 三世諸佛立地聽
Occurrences.AttributionNote: Yunmen's recorded line has the buddhas of the three times stand and listen while flames turn the teaching wheel.

Occurrences.Kwic: 我今立地看你，縱修行百千年，木食草衣，只與吾一般。
Occurrences.AttributionNote: A speaker says, 'I now stand here watching you,' before describing the addressee's long cultivation.

Senses.Explanation: Literally, “plant and steady the heels”; in its primary Chan deployment, “establish firm footing.” The phrase occurs 24 times in 18 allowlisted texts, mainly in later instructions, verses, and public exchanges. One instruction says that in traveling on foot and dwelling in the world one must first “establish firm footing, not be stirred by the eight winds” (立定腳跟，不被八風所鼓). A verse places it as a rock amid vast waves; a public exchange receives the direct interjection, “establish firm footing well” (立定腳跟好). The corpus also corrects a rigid use of the phrase: one master says that always establishing firm footing can, upon close examination, be “a one-sided, withered understanding and a dull fellow who does not comprehend adaptation” (偏枯見解、不達權變之笨漢). Zen therefore bends bodily footing into a recurrent instruction and appraisal for remaining steady, while preserving a recorded warning that immobility itself can be faulted.
Senses.Note: This is distinct from the literal archer’s planted stance below. Different circumstances in which a person is told to remain steady are deployments of one figurative sense, not additional senses.

Occurrences.Kwic: 行腳住世先要立定腳跟，不被八風所鼓。
一向立定腳跟，最怕輥入異類，子細檢點來，正是偏枯見解、不達權變之笨漢。
師云：「立定腳跟好。」進云：「等閒垂一釣，驚動碧波鱗。」
萬頃波中一片石，立定腳跟赤骨歷，縱橫無礙百千般，都緣應化非真實。

Senses.Explanation: The same four graphs also describe a literal bodily stance. Wuyi Yuanlai compares possessing the eye of inquiry to a skilled archer who “plants his heels firmly, then takes up the bow and sets the arrow, and only then can hit the target” (立定腳跟，然後拈弓架箭，始能中的). Here the phrase names what the archer physically does before shooting, not a second reading of figurative steadiness.
Senses.Note: One independent allowlisted source in the researched concordance clearly anchors this physical referent, so the sense remains provisional. It is placed second because the Zen-loaded figurative sense is primary in this corpus.

Occurrences.Kwic: 譬如善射者，立定腳跟，然後拈弓架箭，始能中的也。

Senses.PreferredTarget: where you stand is all genuine
AlternateTargets: the place you take is entirely real
Senses.Explanation: Literally, at the place of standing or taking one's position (立處), all is genuine or real (皆真): "where you stand is all genuine." It occurs 35 times in 24 allowlisted texts. Linji's record supplies the governing formula twice: "act as host wherever you are; where you stand is all genuine; arriving circumstances cannot turn you around" (隨處作主，立處皆真，境來回換不得). The second passage precedes it with "do not receive another person's delusion" and follows it by warning that a single doubtful thought gives an opening. Later records reverse its paired order as "where you stand is all genuine; act as host according to the place" (立處皆真，隨方作主), attach it to "take it up and immediately use it" (拈來便用), and explicitly quote Linji's wording as "bring it and immediately use it; where you stand is all genuine" (把來便用，立處皆真). Chan bends the ordinary idea of a standing-place into a stable Linji roster phrase about taking the host position amid changing circumstances; the entry reports the formula and its transmitted predicates without adding a claim beyond those recorded predicates.
Senses.Note: The variant "where you stand is immediately genuine" (立處即真) occurs 19 times in 15 texts. The wording is shared beyond Linji quotations, so no master-specific SenseKey is needed.

Occurrences.Kwic: 爾且隨處作主，立處皆真，境來回換不得
Occurrences.AttributionNote: Linji's own record preserves the central three-part formula.

Occurrences.Kwic: 直要不受人惑，隨處作主，立處皆真，但有來者皆不得受。
Occurrences.AttributionNote: Linji's second formulation foregrounds not receiving another person's delusion.

Occurrences.Kwic: 道無動靜法本隨緣。立處皆真隨方作主。
Occurrences.AttributionNote: Huiwen reverses the order of the two Linji clauses.

Occurrences.Kwic: 若能取捨俱忘，觸目無滯，拈來便用，立處皆真
Occurrences.AttributionNote: A later high-seat passage pairs the phrase with taking up and immediately using.

Occurrences.Kwic: 我這裏是活祖師西來意，把來便用，立處皆真。
Occurrences.AttributionNote: The passage explicitly introduces this as Linji's saying and pairs it with immediate use.

Senses.Explanation: Literally, to stand in snow. In the Chan record the phrase predominantly names Huike's vigil before Bodhidharma: Shen-guang stands unmoving through a night of heavy snow until it rises above his knees, and Bodhidharma asks, “You have stood long in the snow; what do you seek?” (汝久立雪中，當求何事). Retrospective formulas join “standing in the snow” with “cutting off the arm” (立雪斷臂), transmission of the robe and bowl, and Huike's request for the buddhas' essential way. Later masters preserve conflicting appraisals: one says, “standing in snow was not yet toil; cutting off the arm was the real thing,” while another calls “the Second Patriarch standing in snow to seek mind” unworthy. It also becomes a stock public question—“what is the meaning of the Second Patriarch standing waist-deep in snow?”—to which the quoted master answers, “a leap month comes once in three years.” The ordinary weather action has thus become the compact name of a lineage encounter and a recurring interview prompt.
Senses.Note: The allowlisted concordance has 507 matches in 186 texts. This sense covers the full narrative, the fixed standing-snow/cut-arm formula, transmission retrospective, later praise and criticism, and a direct public question. Standing-snow/cut-arm (立雪斷臂), the Second Patriarch standing in snow (二祖立雪), and standing waist-deep in snow (立雪齊腰) all name or appraise the same Huike event. Family revalidation with cutting off the arm (斷臂), facing a wall (面壁), transmitting the robe (傳衣), Huike, and Bodhidharma preserves that event as the Zen-loaded primary sense.

Occurrences.Kwic: 其年十二月九日夜。天大雨雪。光堅立不動。遲明積雪過膝。祖憫而問曰。汝久立雪中。當求何事。
Occurrences.AttributionNote: The narrative says Shen-guang stands unmoving through heavy night snow until it rises above his knees; Bodhidharma asks, ‘You have stood long in the snow; what do you seek?’

Occurrences.Kwic: 有神光法師，立雪斷臂，堅求諸佛要道，師為易名慧可。
Occurrences.AttributionNote: A transmission retrospective joins the two actions: ‘Master Shen-guang stood in the snow and cut off his arm, firmly seeking the buddhas' essential way’; Bodhidharma renamed him Huike.

Occurrences.Kwic: 問。如何是西來的的意。師曰。立雪未為勞。斷臂方為的。
Occurrences.AttributionNote: Asked the exact meaning of coming from the West, the master says, ‘Standing in snow was not yet toil; cutting off the arm was the real thing.’

Occurrences.Kwic: 達磨九年面壁，鬼魅之由。二祖立雪求心，飜成不肖。
Occurrences.AttributionNote: A later master criticizes both stock acts: ‘Bodhidharma's nine years facing a wall—the source of ghosts; the Second Patriarch standing in snow to seek mind—turned into unworthiness.’

Occurrences.Kwic: 問：二祖立雪齊腰，意旨如何？師曰：三年逢一閏。曰：為甚麼付法傳衣？師曰：村酒足人酤。
Occurrences.AttributionNote: A monk asks, ‘What is the meaning of the Second Patriarch standing waist-deep in snow?’ The master answers, ‘A leap month comes once in three years,’ then answers a follow-up about transmitting the teaching and robe.

Senses.Explanation: The same graphs also describe the physical posture of a bird in a snowy scene. A master answers a question about proceeding within the four deportments with “a heron stands in the snow” (鷺鶿立雪). A verse separately compares a heron standing in snow with the bright moon and reed flowers. In these passages the subject is a heron and the phrase denotes its visible posture, not Huike's lineage encounter.
Senses.Note: The heron forms (鷺鶿 and 鷺鷥) are graphic variants within one physical-action family. The direct answer and the verse comparison are different deployments of the same bird-and-snow scene, not further senses.

Occurrences.Kwic: 問四威儀中如何履踐。師曰。鷺鶿立雪。曰恁麼則聞鐘持鉢日上闌干。
Occurrences.AttributionNote: Asked, ‘How does one proceed within the four deportments?’ the master says, ‘A heron stands in the snow.’

Occurrences.Kwic: 鷺鷥立雪非同色，明月蘆花不似他。
Occurrences.AttributionNote: The verse says, ‘A heron standing in snow is not of the same color; the bright moon and reed flowers are not alike.’

Senses.Explanation: Literally, request an increase or benefit; in Chan records, ask a teacher for further instruction or clarification. The expression occurs 1,659 times in 286 allowlisted texts. It is used as a verb with the person asked, in biographies of travel from one teacher to another, and after an encounter when an attendant follows a master into his quarters to ask about what was said. Speakers also announce, 'I have come especially to request further instruction.' The Blue Cliff Record gives two explicit genre descriptions. It calls the condition of a long-standing student who has seen but not penetrated, or penetrated but not clarified, 'requesting further instruction'; elsewhere it says that the opening part of a particular monk's question is called requesting further instruction, then separately calls it a question presenting understanding and a concealed-edge question. A later list of question types asks, 'What is a request-for-instruction question?' and receives the answer, 'The monastery gate is wide open.'
Senses.Note: The 23 strings ending in 'one who requests further instruction' mostly count or describe inquirers; they are not graph-formula definitions. The term can name the act, the inquirer, or a classified question. One lamp exchange explicitly contrasts obtaining something by reading texts, obtaining it by requesting instruction, and obtaining it by neither.

Occurrences.AttributionNote: A two-speaker lamp exchange contrasts getting something from reading texts, from requesting instruction, and from neither.

Occurrences.AttributionNote: A biography uses the verb with its requested teacher and records that the teacher responded with a verse.

Senses.Explanation: Śākyamuni, the name by which the Chan corpus identifies the buddha of its founding cases. The Ancestral Hall Collection gives the in-corpus name gloss: “Śākyamuni: translated, it says ‘Able and Benevolent’” (釋迦者，譯言能仁也). The record then bends the name through case and appraisal. It names Śākyamuni as the one who holds up the flower before Kāśyapa’s smile and as the one who mounts the seat before Mañjuśrī strikes the sounding block. It also makes him the subject of public questions: Yunmen answers “What is Śākyamuni’s body?” (如何是釋迦身) with “a dry shit-stick” (乾屎橛). Other recorded appraisals are equally direct: Guoqing Feng calls Śākyamuni “an ox-headed jailer” (牛頭獄卒), and Shaoshan describes him as “the general of a defeated army” (敗軍之將), alongside Kāśyapa as “a man who has lost his life” (喪身失命底人). Nantái Yungong says, “Śākyamuni has already perished; Maitreya has not yet been born” (釋迦已滅，彌勒未生), then raises the whisk and locates the handling of the buddha-teaching in that day’s teaching seat. The deviation is this range: the proper name is not protected as a remote sacred biography; it is a recurrent actor in the flower and seat cases, a subject put into public questions, and a figure whom masters openly compare, re-stage, and appraise.
Senses.Note: The 6,608 exact matches occur in 395 allowlisted files. “Śākyamuni” is the name-form. “The World-Honored One” (世尊) is a title used heavily in the flower, seat, and silence cases; “old man Śākyamuni” (釋迦老子) is a longer familiar form with its own strongly marked Chan deployment. Matches inside the longer form overlap mechanically but do not erase that lexical distinction.

Occurrences.Kwic: 姓釋迦。釋迦者，譯言能仁也。
Occurrences.AttributionNote: Ancestral Hall Collection; the passage itself gives the name gloss: “The surname was Śākyamuni. Śākyamuni, translated, means ‘Able and Benevolent.’”

Occurrences.Kwic: 當時釋迦拈花何等直捷？迦葉微笑何等快便？
Occurrences.AttributionNote: Record of Master Zhu Yuheng of Purple Bamboo Grove; a later address explicitly pairs “Śākyamuni held up the flower” with “Kāśyapa smiled,” appraising the former as direct and the latter as quick.

Occurrences.Kwic: 問如何是釋迦身。師云。乾屎橛。
Occurrences.AttributionNote: Extended Record of Yunmen; in a public question, “What is Śākyamuni’s body?”, Yunmen answers, “A dry shit-stick.”

Occurrences.Kwic: 問：如何是佛法大意？師云：釋迦是牛頭獄卒，祖師是馬面阿傍。
Occurrences.AttributionNote: Linked Lamp Collection, Guoqing Feng section; asked the main meaning of the buddha-teaching, Feng says, “Śākyamuni is an ox-headed jailer; the ancestral teacher is a horse-faced attendant.”

Occurrences.Kwic: 我道釋迦是敗軍之將。迦葉是喪身失命底人。
Occurrences.AttributionNote: Transmission of the Lamp; Shaoshan says, “I say Śākyamuni is the general of a defeated army; Kāśyapa is a man who has lost his life.” This is a direct recorded appraisal, not an annotator’s interpretation.

Occurrences.Kwic: 何謂釋迦已滅，彌勒未生？拈起拂子云：正當今日，佛法盡在山僧拂子頭上放行把住，一切臨時。
Occurrences.AttributionNote: Linked Lamp Collection, Nantái Yungong section; he says, “Śākyamuni has already perished; Maitreya has not yet been born,” raises the whisk, and says that today the buddha-teaching’s releasing and holding are entirely at the end of his whisk.

Occurrences.Kwic: 豈不見釋迦陞座，文殊白椎，馬祖陞堂，百丈捲席
Occurrences.AttributionNote: Eryin Mi's record; Śākyamuni mounting the seat and Mañjuśrī striking the block are placed beside Mazu mounting the hall and Baizhang rolling up the mat. This anchors Śākyamuni as an actor in the teaching-seat case, not as outside biography.

Occurrences.Kwic: 衲僧家高揖釋迦，不拜彌勒，未為分外。
Occurrences.AttributionNote: Five Lamps Complete Collection, Fayun Faxiu section; for patch-robed monks to salute Śākyamuni from on high and not bow to Maitreya is still not beyond their part. This anchors the masters' direct handling of the named figure.

Occurrences.Kwic: 問：一塵一佛國，一葉一釋迦。學人如何下足？師曰：大地草漫漫。
Occurrences.AttributionNote: Five Lamps Complete Collection, Caoshan Baoji Xiong section; 'one buddha-land in a mote, one Śākyamuni on a leaf' becomes the premise of a public question about where the student can set foot. The named figure is deployed inside the interview's scale-making image.

Occurrences.Kwic: 釋迦之為釋迦，非增也；木石之為木石，非滅也。
Occurrences.AttributionNote: Hefeng's record, teaching-seat address; 'Śākyamuni being Śākyamuni is no increase; wood and stone being wood and stone is no decrease.' The name is set directly beside ordinary things in a recorded contrast.

Senses.Explanation: Literally, “old man Śākyamuni.” In the Chan record this familiar name-form removes formal distance: masters quote what “old man Śākyamuni said,” stage his arrival with a staff or whisk, claim to speak where he could not, threaten him with blows, and attach coarse appraisals to his name. Longji Shaoxiu raises his staff and cries, “Old man Śākyamuni has arrived!” (釋迦老子來也) as his answer to “What is great function appearing?” (如何是大用現前). Dahui Zonggao likewise raises the whisk and says that the old man has arrived, then asks whether the assembly sees him. In another record, a master says that even if old man Śākyamuni came there, he would receive thirty blows; Dahui comments on a story of Śākyamuni disputing the buddha-teaching with Indra by saying, “This old fellow deserves thirty staff-blows” (這老漢好與三十拄杖). The form also remains a quotation label: Yunmen says, “Old man Śākyamuni has already spoken; Maitreya still does not know” (釋迦老子道了也，彌勒猶自不知). A later master says, “Speak a sentence where old man Śākyamuni could not speak; take a step where the great teacher Bodhidharma could not go” (釋迦老子說不到處，說取一句；達磨大師行不到處，行取一步). The strongest coarse appraisal is textual and explicit: “Śākyamuni is a dry shit-stick” (釋迦老子是乾屎橛), paired with “Mañjuśrī and Samantabhadra are shit-carrying fellows” (文殊普賢是擔屎漢). The deviation lies in the form’s repeated Chan use: a revered name becomes an immediately addressable “old man” whom masters quote, enact, out-say, rebuke, and strike in public discourse.
Senses.Note: The exact longer form occurs 2,409 times in 281 allowlisted files. The suffix “old man” (老子) is translated rather than omitted: it is what distinguishes this headword from bare “Śākyamuni” (釋迦). The examples preserve separate deployment classes—quotation label, enacted arrival, comparison, rebuke, and coarse appraisal—rather than treating every overlap with the shorter name as equivalent.

Occurrences.Kwic: 達磨是老臊胡。釋迦老子是乾屎橛。文殊普賢是擔屎漢。
Occurrences.AttributionNote: Five Lamps United at the Source; a recorded address says, “Bodhidharma is an old stinking foreigner; old man Śākyamuni is a dry shit-stick; Mañjuśrī and Samantabhadra are shit-carrying fellows.” The entry reports the wording without assigning an unspoken intent.

Occurrences.Kwic: 大用現前。不存軌則。時有僧問。如何是大用現前。師拈起拄杖。高聲唱曰。釋迦老子來也。
Occurrences.AttributionNote: Five Lamps United at the Source, Longji Shaoxiu section; asked “What is great function appearing?”, Longji raises his staff and loudly cries, “Old man Śākyamuni has arrived!”

Occurrences.Kwic: 復舉起云。釋迦老子來也。還見麼。
Occurrences.AttributionNote: Record of Dahui Pujue; after striking the Chan seat with the whisk and raising it again, Dahui says, “Old man Śākyamuni has arrived! Do you see him?”

Occurrences.Kwic: 直饒釋迦老子到這裏也與三十棒
Occurrences.AttributionNote: Recorded Sayings of the Old Worthies; the master says, “Even if old man Śākyamuni came here, I would give him thirty blows.” The nearby section heading identifies the Fengxue lineage material, but the occurrence is left unattributed because the rough head pointer is not a secure speaker label.

Occurrences.Kwic: 師云釋迦老子道了也彌勒猶自不知
Occurrences.AttributionNote: Recorded Sayings of the Old Worthies; after an elder asks how to discern at all times, Yunmen says, “Old man Śākyamuni has already spoken; Maitreya still does not know.”

Occurrences.Kwic: 釋迦老子說不到處，說取一句；達磨大師行不到處，行取一步。
Occurrences.AttributionNote: Record of Chan Master Shanhui; in a small address the master says, “Speak a sentence where old man Śākyamuni could not speak; take a step where the great teacher Bodhidharma could not go.”

Occurrences.Kwic: 釋迦老子與天帝釋。在中庭裏相爭佛法甚鬧。師云。這老漢好與三十拄杖。
Occurrences.AttributionNote: Record of Dahui Pujue; after raising Yunmen’s saying that old man Śākyamuni and Indra were noisily disputing the buddha-teaching in the courtyard, Dahui says, “This old fellow deserves thirty staff-blows.”
